lead: A sender can push electrons along copper, flash light down glass, or launch a wave into the air. Copper and glass are guided: the signal stays inside a solid path. Air is unguided: antennas launch and catch the wave. Bandwidth, loss, distance, cost and noise immunity decide which medium a link uses.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for wavelength and frequency, and 2.2 for attenuation in dB.

sections.h3: Guided media: twisted pair and coaxial

blocks.text: A guided medium is a solid path, copper or glass, that keeps the signal inside it.

Twisted pair is two insulated copper wires twisted together. Both pick up nearly the same noise, and the receiver takes the difference, so shared noise cancels. More twists per metre cancel better. Unshielded twisted pair (UTP) has no foil. Shielded twisted pair (STP) wraps the pairs in metal foil, which blocks interference; STP costs more and is stiffer.

items: Cat 3: up to 16 MHz, telephone wiring and 10 Mbps Ethernet.
Cat 5e: up to 100 MHz, 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps Ethernet.
Cat 6: up to 250 MHz, 1 Gbps to 100 m, 10 Gbps only over shorter runs.

blocks.text: UTP ends in an RJ-45 plug, the clip-in connector on every LAN cable. Ethernet over UTP stops at 100 m per run, because the signal attenuates and the pairs pick up noise beyond that. The cable is cheap, flexible and easy to terminate.

Coaxial cable has a central copper conductor, a plastic insulator, a braided metal shield and an outer jacket. The grounded shield blocks outside fields, so coaxial has better noise immunity and more bandwidth than twisted pair. A 50 Ω cable carries one baseband digital signal; a 75 Ω cable carries many modulated channels, as in cable TV and cable internet.

An optical fibre is a glass core of refractive index n₁ surrounded by cladding of slightly lower index n₂. Light entering within a small cone hits the boundary at a shallow angle and reflects back completely. This is total internal reflection, so loss is tiny.

blocks.where: θc is the critical angle, measured inside the core from the normal to the boundary; n₁ is the core refractive index; n₂ is the cladding refractive index, with n₁ > n₂. A ray is guided only if its angle of incidence at the boundary exceeds θc.
NA is the numerical aperture, how much light the fibre accepts; θa is the acceptance angle, the largest half-angle of the cone at the fibre face that is still guided.

blocks.text: A step-index fibre has one cladding index, so rays zig-zag over different lengths and arrive at different times; this is modal dispersion. A graded-index fibre lowers the index gradually, so outer rays curve and travel faster, narrowing the spread. Single-mode fibre has an 8–10 µm core, one path, a laser source, and reaches tens of kilometres. Multimode fibre has a 50 or 62.5 µm core and an LED source, and covers a building or campus.

Fibre joins use LC, SC or ST connectors, or a fusion splice that melts the ends into one. Fibre gives huge bandwidth, no crosstalk, no electromagnetic interference and very low attenuation, which is why Indian backbones and fibre-to-the-home networks use it. It is fragile, and splicing needs a fusion splicer.

sections.h3: Unguided media: radio, microwave and infrared

blocks.text: An unguided medium is free space, air or vacuum. No cable contains the signal, so antennas launch and receive it and it spreads as it travels.

items: Radio waves, about 3 kHz to 1 GHz, are omnidirectional: the transmitter sends in all directions and the receiver need not be aimed. They pass through walls, so they serve broadcast radio, TV and indoor wireless. Below about 2 MHz they travel as ground waves; between 2 and 30 MHz they bounce off the ionosphere as sky waves.

Microwaves, about 1 GHz to 300 GHz, are directional. A parabolic dish focuses the beam, so dishes must point at each other and the path must be clear. Terrestrial links hop 40–50 km between towers. A geostationary satellite sits about 36,000 km up: the one-way delay is about a quarter of a second, so a round-trip conversation is delayed by about half a second. Three such satellites cover most of the planet, and VSAT dishes bring banking and internet to remote villages.
Infrared, about 300 GHz to 400 THz, works indoors over a few metres. It does not pass through walls, so it cannot leak between rooms; remote controls use it.

blocks.text: Above 30 MHz, radio and microwave links use line-of-sight propagation: both antennas must see each other. The earth curves, so a taller antenna sees farther; that sets tower height and hop length.

examples.question: A step-index fibre has core refractive index n₁ = 1.50 and cladding refractive index n₂ = 1.48. Find (a) the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary, (b) the numerical aperture, and (c) the acceptance angle at the fibre face.
steps: Data: n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.48. Since n₁ > n₂, total internal reflection is possible.
sin θc = n₂ / n₁ = 1.48 / 1.50 = 0.9867, so θc = 80.63°, measured inside the core from the normal to the boundary.
θa = sin⁻¹(0.2441) = 14.13°. Light entering the face inside a cone of half-angle 14.13°, about 28.3° total, is guided.
examples.answer: The critical angle is 80.63°, the numerical aperture is 0.2441, and the acceptance angle is 14.13°.
examples.check:
import math
n1 = 1.50
n2 = 1.48
theta_c = math.degrees(math.asin(n2 / n1))
NA = math.sqrt(n1**2 - n2**2)
theta_a = math.degrees(math.asin(NA))
print(round(theta_c, 2))
print(round(NA, 4))
print(round(theta_a, 2))

examples.question: A campus needs a 2 Gbps link between two buildings 3 km apart, with no repeater allowed between them. Which guided medium fits, and why?
steps: Twisted pair is out: Cat 6 carries 1 Gbps only to 100 m, and 3 km is 30 times that limit.
Coaxial is out: its bandwidth is a few hundred MHz and it too needs repeaters over 3 km.
Multimode fibre carries about 1 Gbps to a few hundred metres because of modal dispersion, so 3 km is too far.
Single-mode fibre with a laser reaches tens of kilometres at 10 Gbps and more, with no repeater and no crosstalk.
examples.answer: Single-mode optical fibre: it gives 2 Gbps over 3 km without a repeater, with no crosstalk and immunity to electromagnetic interference.

traps: Swapping the acceptance angle and the critical angle. The critical angle is inside the fibre at the core–cladding boundary; the acceptance angle is outside, at the fibre face.
Thinking total internal reflection works both ways. Light must start in the denser core, with n₁ > n₂.
Reading 'single mode' as 'one direction'. It means one propagation path; a single-mode link still needs two strands for full duplex.
Quoting the 100 m UTP limit as a limit of twisted pair in general. It is an Ethernet cabling standard set by attenuation and noise.
Confusing 50 Ω with 75 Ω coaxial cable. 50 Ω is baseband, one digital signal; 75 Ω is broadband, many channels as in cable TV.

quiz.q: State the difference between guided and unguided transmission media, with one example of each.
quiz.a: Guided media confine the signal to a solid path, for example twisted pair, coaxial cable or optical fibre. Unguided media send the signal through free space, for example radio waves or infrared, and need antennas.

quiz.q: Name the four parts of a coaxial cable and the connector used on a UTP LAN cable.
quiz.a: Central copper conductor, plastic insulator, braided metal shield, outer jacket. UTP LAN cable uses an RJ-45 plug.

quiz.q: Why does twisting the two wires of a pair reduce noise, while a shield works by a different mechanism?
quiz.a: Twisting makes both wires pick up nearly equal noise voltages, and the receiver reads the difference, so the shared noise cancels. A shield is grounded metal foil around the pairs; it blocks outside fields, so noise is prevented rather than cancelled.

quiz.q: A step-index fibre has n₁ = 1.52 and n₂ = 1.50. Find the critical angle, the numerical aperture and the acceptance angle.
Why must two microwave dishes point at each other, while a radio broadcast antenna need not be aimed at any one receiver?
quiz.a: Microwave links use parabolic dishes that focus energy into a narrow line-of-sight beam; misaligned dishes miss it. Radio broadcast uses omnidirectional antennas that radiate in all directions, so any receiver in the coverage area picks up the signal.

quiz.q: A fibre link and a coaxial link have the same length. Explain why the fibre carries far more data with far less error.
quiz.a: Fibre guides light by total internal reflection inside the core, so outside fields do not affect the signal and none leaks between strands; this removes electromagnetic interference and crosstalk. Its attenuation per kilometre is much lower, so the signal stays above the noise floor farther. The optical carrier is around 10¹⁴ Hz, giving enormous bandwidth, and wavelength division multiplexing shares that band among many channels. Coaxial carries an electrical signal, picks up fields through its shield, and its usable band is only a few hundred MHz.

quiz.q: A hill station 60 km from the nearest town needs internet. Compare a terrestrial microwave hop with a satellite link on delay, cost and dependence on terrain.
quiz.a: A terrestrial hop needs a clear line of sight between towers and a tower on the hill, so terrain decides feasibility, but delay is only microseconds and equipment cost is moderate. A geostationary satellite link ignores terrain and covers remote areas, but adds about a quarter of a second of delay one way, which hurts voice and interactive traffic, and terminal charges are higher. If line of sight is possible, microwave wins on delay and cost; otherwise satellite is the fallback.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fibre to the home uses passive optical networks, where one laser in the exchange is split by passive splitters to many homes, and dense wavelength division multiplexing pushes terabits per second down a backbone strand. Data centres run multimode fibre between racks and single-mode between buildings. Free-space optics sends a laser beam through the air between rooftops, and fails in fog and dust. Low-earth-orbit satellite constellations cut the quarter-second delay of geostationary links by flying at a few hundred kilometres.
